# Dynamic report

## Tracking data related to studying at a desk at home

### Data Collection

I collected this data using Google Forms, with three main questions:

1.  How long did you study for?

-   This was to the closest 10 minutes. I used regex to make sure answers were provided in digits and ending in the number 0.

2.  What paper was the majority of the time spent studying?

-   I am doing 4 papers this semester, so I gave the options of PSYCH 200, PSYCH 202, PSYCH 207 and STATS 220.

3.  What mode of learning did I use primarily?

-   The options were digital and paper.

### Overall findings (dynamic comments and bar charts)

These were the findings, compiled in RStudio:

```{r}
# I have no idea if I'm doing this right but I will copy paste the code that will produce the 2 summary values and 2 bar charts that I want

library(tidyverse)

logged_data <- read_csv("https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/e/2PACX-1vQsrhn0TjCxddW92JsbZNktkmBpDePrsQiFpVsIaFOQfwe-FKyOUREwBjJjZDUYRMwNzJ6S2DGUFAXN/pub?gid=627355158&single=true&output=csv")

# renaming

latest_data <- logged_data %>%
  rename (time_spent = 4,
          paper_studied = 5,
          learning_mode = 6) 

clean_data_frame <- latest_data %>%
  na.omit()


# my summary values - the maximum time spent studying and the mean time spent studying

maximum_time_spent <- max(clean_data_frame$time_spent)

mean_time_spent <- mean(clean_data_frame$time_spent) %>%
  round(0)

# creating a sentence

summary_text <- paste("The longest time spent studying at a desk was", 
      max(clean_data_frame$time_spent),
      "minutes.", 
      "The mean time spent studying at a desk was", 
      mean(clean_data_frame$time_spent) %>%
        round(0),
      "minutes", 
      collapse = " ")

# Now time for my bar charts. The first one compares the frequency of when I study each paper.



graph_1 <- ggplot(data = clean_data_frame) +
  geom_bar(aes(y = paper_studied),
           fill = "#b94aed",
           color = "#895B7B",) +
  labs(title = "Most Studied Papers",
       subtitle = "Comparing the frequency of Ella Hermann's university papers studying at a desk at home in Semester One 2026",
       caption = "Source: Google Forms",
       x = "Paper Studied",
       y = "Number of times this paper was the most studied")

# The second graph is a distribution of the time I spent studying
  
graph_2 <- ggplot(data = clean_data_frame) + 
    geom_bar(aes(x = learning_mode),
             fill = "#29beb2",
             color = "#888888") +
    theme(
      panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#f2c7e6")
    ) +
    labs(title = "Distribution of Time Spent Studying",
         subtitle = "Comparing the distribution of learning modes Ella Hermann has used studying her university papers at a desk at home in Semester One 2026",
         caption = "Source: Google Forms",
         x = "Mode of learning",
         y = "frequency")
  
###### here are my final summary values and graphs. my reasoning for using this data is above
summary_text
graph_1
graph_2
```

### Dynamic Comments

These dynamic comments reflect: 1. The longest time in minutes spent studying at a desk at home 2. The mean amount of time spent studying at a desk at home, in minutes

Together, these were compiled into a singular dynamic comment, which changes as the data is updated. The comment can be seen below:

```{r}
paste(summary_text)

```

### Most Studied Papers

The first bar chart represents how many instances each paper was the most studied one. This will help me work out what papers I'm prioritising, and what ones I should study more.

The first bar chart can be seen below:

```{r}
print(graph_1)
```

### Distribution of Time Spent Studying

The second bar chart represents the distribution of the amount of time I spent studying at my desk at home. This will help me work out what the more common lengths of studying are, and how long (or short) some of my study sessions are.

The second bar chart can be seen below:

```{r}
print(graph_2)
```
